db.er-tables.title: ER model to relations: minimum number of tables
db.er-tables.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.er-tables.check: Strong entity: 1 table. M:N and n-ary: own table. 1:N: FK on the N side. 1:1: FK on either side (one table if total on both). Weak entity: own table, key = owner key + partial key. Multivalued attribute: own table. Composite: flatten.

db.keys.title: Keys, NULLs and referential integrity
db.keys.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.keys.check: Superkey = any set containing a key; count with inclusion-exclusion. PK: unique and NOT NULL. FK: matches a referenced key or is NULL. Trace ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL row by row.

db.ra-eval.title: Evaluate relational algebra on small tables
db.ra-eval.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.ra-eval.check: Apply σ row by row, then π removes duplicate tuples (set semantics). Join count = Σ over common values of (matches in R)×(matches in S). ∪/∩/− need whole-tuple equality.

db.ra-division.title: Division R ÷ S
db.ra-division.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.ra-division.check: R(A,B) ÷ S(B) keeps a value a when (a, b) ∈ R for EVERY b in S. Formula: π_A(R) − π_A((π_A(R) × S) − R). Empty S returns π_A(R).

db.ra-equiv.title: Reading and rewriting algebra expressions
db.ra-equiv.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.ra-equiv.check: σ cascades and commutes; σ_{p∨q} = σ_p ∪ σ_q; π does not distribute over −; a σ after a join tests one joined tuple, so both conditions refer to the same row.

db.trc.title: Tuple relational calculus: reading and safety
db.trc.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.trc.check: ∃ = at least one, ¬∃ = none, ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) = every x satisfying P also satisfies Q. A query is safe only if every answer comes from values in the database.

db.sql-joins.title: SQL joins: inner and outer row counts
db.sql-joins.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.sql-joins.check: Inner join: Σ matches; LEFT adds unmatched left rows; FULL adds both sides' unmatched rows. NULL = NULL is never true in ON. A filter on the right table in WHERE undoes a LEFT JOIN.

db.sql-subquery.title: Subqueries: IN, EXISTS, ALL, ANY, scalar
db.sql-subquery.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.sql-subquery.check: > ALL = greater than the maximum, > ANY = greater than the minimum. NOT IN over a list containing NULL returns no rows; NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe. IN does not duplicate outer rows; a join can.

db.sql-groupby.title: GROUP BY, HAVING and aggregates with NULL
db.sql-groupby.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.sql-groupby.check: Order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) and AVG/SUM skip NULL. All NULL keys form one group.

db.sql-null.title: NULL, three-valued logic, DISTINCT and boundaries
db.sql-null.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.sql-null.check: Comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN; WHERE keeps only TRUE. TRUE OR UNKNOWN = TRUE, FALSE AND UNKNOWN = FALSE, NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. DISTINCT treats NULLs as one value. BETWEEN is inclusive.

db.fd-closure.title: Attribute closure, implied FDs and minimal cover
db.fd-closure.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.fd-closure.check: X⁺: start from X and keep firing every FD whose whole LHS is inside the set. X → Y holds iff Y ⊆ X⁺. Minimal cover: split RHS, drop extraneous LHS attributes, then drop redundant FDs.

db.fd-keys.title: Candidate keys, prime attributes and superkeys
db.fd-keys.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.fd-keys.check: Attributes never on any RHS belong to every key. Grow from them, test closures, keep only minimal sets, and keep searching after the first key.

db.nf-test.title: 2NF, 3NF, BCNF tests and highest normal form
db.nf-test.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.nf-test.check: Find all keys first. BCNF: every nontrivial X → A has X a superkey. 3NF: or A is prime. 2NF: no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a key.

db.decomp.title: Lossless join and dependency preservation
db.decomp.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.decomp.check: Binary split R1, R2 is lossless iff (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or (R1 ∩ R2) → R2. Preservation: each FD must follow from the FDs projected onto the parts, without joining them.

db.bplus-order.title: B/B+ tree order, capacity and height
db.bplus-order.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.bplus-order.check: Internal B+ node: p·P_block + (p−1)·K ≤ B. Leaf: n·(K + P_rec) + P_next ≤ B. B-tree node also stores a data pointer per key. Max keys with h levels: p^(h−1)·(leaf keys); min uses root ≥ 2 and ⌈p/2⌉ elsewhere.

db.index-access.title: Index size and block-access counts
db.index-access.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.index-access.check: bfr = ⌊B / record⌋. Sparse (primary) index: one entry per data block; dense: one per record; clustering: one per distinct value. Multilevel: divide by the index bfr until one block; accesses = levels + 1 data block.

db.index-types.title: Dense, sparse, clustering, secondary; B+ tree vs hash
db.index-types.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.index-types.check: One physical order per file: at most one primary or clustering index, many secondary (always dense). Hash: equality only. B+ tree: equality and range via linked leaves.

db.dw-schema.title: Star/snowflake schemas, measures, hierarchies and OLAP operations
db.dw-schema.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.dw-schema.check: Fact table = foreign keys to dimensions + numeric measures. Snowflake normalizes dimensions (more tables, more joins). Roll-up climbs a hierarchy, drill-down descends, slice fixes one dimension, dice restricts several.

db.olap-cube.title: OLAP cube and CUBE/ROLLUP row counts
db.olap-cube.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.olap-cube.check: n dimensions: 2ⁿ cuboids; with Lᵢ hierarchy levels: Π(Lᵢ + 1). CUBE rows with all combinations present: Π(nᵢ + 1). ROLLUP(a, b): (a, b) + (a) + (). With missing combinations, count distinct groups per grouping set.

db.transform.title: Normalization and discretization
db.transform.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.transform.check: Min-max: (v − min)/(max − min)·(new range) + new min. Z-score: (v − μ)/σ. Decimal scaling: v/10ʲ with the smallest j giving max|v'| < 1. Equal-width bins: width = (max − min)/k.

db.sampling.title: Sampling and data reduction
db.sampling.subject: Database Management and Warehousing
db.sampling.check: SRSWOR: C(N, s) samples, P(tuple chosen) = s/N. SRSWR: P = 1 − (1 − 1/N)ˢ. Stratified: proportional share per stratum. Cluster: pick whole groups.

questions.stem:
An ER diagram has three strong entity sets:

- E1 with key `a` and a **multivalued** attribute `phone`,
- E2 with key `b` and a **composite** attribute `addr(street, city)`,
- E3 with key `c`.

Relationship R12 between E1 and E2 is many-to-many. Relationship R23 between E2 and E3 is one-to-many (one E2 to many E3), with partial participation on both sides. What is the minimum number of tables needed for a relational schema in 1NF?

options.why: Gave the one-to-many R23 its own table; its key b can go into E3 as a foreign key.
Made tables for both R23 and the composite attribute; a composite attribute is flattened into columns.
E1, E1_phone, E2 (street and city flattened), E3 (with FK b for R23) and R12(a, b).
Kept `phone` as a column of E1; a multivalued attribute breaks 1NF and needs its own table (a, phone).

questions.solution:
1. One table each for E1, E2, E3.
2. Multivalued `phone` -> extra table (a, phone).
3. M:N R12 -> table (a, b).
4. 1:N R23 -> FK `b` in E3; composite `addr` -> columns street, city.
5. Total 5.

questions.stem:
Strong entity sets: Employee (key `eid`) and Project (key `pid`).

- Dependent is a **weak** entity set owned by Employee through the identifying relationship Has (one employee, many dependents).
- WorksOn is a many-to-many relationship between Employee and Project.
- Manages is a one-to-one relationship between Employee and Project with partial participation on both sides.

What is the minimum number of tables in the relational schema?

traps.why: Created tables for the identifying relationship Has and for the 1:1 Manages as well.
Created a table for one of Has or Manages; both fold into an existing table.
Folded the weak entity into Employee; a weak entity with many instances per owner needs its own table.

questions.solution:
1. Employee, Project: 2 tables.
2. Dependent: table (eid, dep_name, ...) with key eid + partial key; Has needs no table.
3. WorksOn (M:N): table (eid, pid).
4. Manages (1:1): FK in either side, no table. Total 4.

questions.stem:
Building (key `bid`) owns the weak entity set Room, whose partial key is `room_no`. Guest has key `gid`. The relationship Booked between Room and Guest is many-to-many and has a descriptive attribute `date`; a guest books a given room at most once.

What is the primary key of the table for Booked?

options.why: Added the descriptive attribute; each (room, guest) pair occurs once, so date is not needed for uniqueness.
Treated Booked as one-to-many; in M:N a guest can appear with many rooms.
A Room is identified by (bid, room_no); an M:N table's key is the union of the participating keys.
Used the partial key alone; room_no repeats across buildings, so a room is identified only by (bid, room_no).

questions.solution:
1. Weak entity key = owner key + partial key = (bid, room_no).
2. M:N table key = keys of both sides = (bid, room_no, gid).
3. `date` is a non-key column because a pair occurs once.

questions.stem: Department (key `did`) and Employee (key `eid`) are linked by WorksIn: each employee works in exactly one department (total participation of Employee) and a department has many employees. Which statements about the minimal relational design are correct?

options.text: WorksIn is represented by adding `did` as a foreign key column in Employee.
options.why: For 1:N the key of the one side goes into the table of the many side.

options.text: The foreign key should go into Department, holding the `eid` of its employees.
options.why: Reversed the direction; Department would then need a multivalued column, which breaks 1NF.

options.text: A minimal design always needs a separate table for every 1:N relationship.
options.why: Over-claim; 1:N folds into the N-side table, and only M:N or n-ary relationships need their own table.

options.text: Because every employee must have a department, that foreign key can be declared NOT NULL.
options.why: Total participation of the N side is enforced by NOT NULL on the foreign key.

questions.solution:
1. 1:N -> FK on the many side: Employee(eid, ..., did).
2. Total participation of Employee -> `did` NOT NULL.
3. No extra table is needed.

questions.stem:
An ER diagram has strong entity sets A, B, C, D (keys a, b, c, d).

- A and B are linked by a one-to-one relationship with **total** participation on **both** sides.
- B and C are linked by a many-to-many relationship.
- C and D are linked by a one-to-many relationship (one C, many D).
- D has a multivalued attribute `tag`.

What is the minimum number of tables?

traps.why: Kept A and B as separate tables; with total participation on both sides of a 1:1 they merge into one table.
Also created a table for the 1:N relationship between C and D, whose key fits in D as a foreign key.
Kept `tag` inside D; a multivalued attribute needs its own table in 1NF.

questions.solution:
1. A + B merge into one table (1:1, total on both sides).
2. C, D: 2 tables; C-D 1:N -> FK c in D.
3. B-C M:N: 1 table; D.tag: 1 table.
4. Total 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5.

questions.stem: Which statements about keys and NULLs in the relational model are correct?

options.text: A relation has exactly one candidate key.
options.why: A relation can have several candidate keys; only one is chosen as primary key.

options.text: No attribute of a primary key may be NULL.
options.why: Entity integrity: a primary key must identify every tuple, so each of its attributes is NOT NULL.

options.text: A foreign key must reference the primary key of a different relation.
options.why: Over-claim; a foreign key may reference its own relation (for example manager_id -> emp_id) and may reference any candidate key.

options.text: A foreign key value may be NULL unless the column is declared NOT NULL.
options.why: Referential integrity requires a match only for non-NULL foreign key values.

questions.solution:
1. Entity integrity: PK attributes are NOT NULL.
2. Referential integrity: an FK is NULL or matches an existing key value.
3. Self-references are allowed; candidate keys can be many.

questions.stem: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has exactly two candidate keys: {A} and {B, C}. How many superkeys does R have?

traps.why: Added 16 + 8 without subtracting the 4 sets that contain both A and BC.
Counted only the supersets of {A}.
Counted candidate keys instead of superkeys.

questions.solution:
1. Supersets of {A}: $2^4 = 16$.
2. Supersets of {B, C}: $2^3 = 8$.
3. Supersets of {A, B, C}: $2^2 = 4$.
4. Inclusion-exclusion: 16 + 8 - 4 = 20.

questions.stem:
Consider this instance of Student.

**Student**

| roll | name | email | dept |
|---|---|---|---|
| 101 | Anu | anu@x | CS |
| 102 | Ravi | ravi@x | EE |
| 103 | Anu | anu2@x | ME |
| 104 | Kiran | kiran@x | CS |

Using **only** this instance, which attribute set can be ruled out as a candidate key?

options.why: roll is unique here, so the instance cannot rule it out (it also cannot prove it is a key).
email is unique here, so this instance gives no evidence against it.
Two different tuples share name = Anu, so {name} cannot be a key of any legal state that includes this instance.
The two Anu rows differ in dept (CS, ME), so the pair is unique in this instance.

questions.solution:
1. An instance can disprove a key (a duplicate value) but never prove one.
2. name repeats (Anu); roll, email and (name, dept) do not.
3. Only {name} is ruled out.

questions.stem:
The tables are created as follows.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Dept (did TEXT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE Emp (eid TEXT PRIMARY KEY, did TEXT REFERENCES Dept(did) ON DELETE CASCADE);
CREATE TABLE Proj (pid TEXT PRIMARY KEY, eid TEXT REFERENCES Emp(eid) ON DELETE SET NULL);
```

**Dept**

| did |
|---|
| d1 |
| d2 |
| d3 |

**Emp**

| eid | did |
|---|---|
| e1 | d1 |
| e2 | d1 |
| e3 | d2 |
| e4 | d1 |
| e5 | d3 |

**Proj**

| pid | eid |
|---|---|
| p1 | e1 |
| p2 | e3 |
| p3 | e2 |
| p4 | e1 |
| p5 | NULL |

After `DELETE FROM Dept WHERE did = 'd1';`, how many rows of Proj have `eid` NULL?

traps.why: Counted only the rows set to NULL by the cascade and forgot p5, which was NULL already.
Assumed SET NULL does not fire when the Emp rows are removed by a cascade; cascaded deletes trigger the referencing actions too.
Stopped at Emp: thought deleting from Dept cannot affect Proj.

questions.solution:
1. Deleting d1 cascades to Emp rows e1, e2, e4.
2. Each deleted employee triggers ON DELETE SET NULL in Proj: p1, p3, p4 become NULL.
3. p5 was already NULL, so 4 rows have NULL eid.

questions.stem: Emp(eid, did) has a foreign key `did` referencing Dept(did) with no referential action (the default RESTRICT / NO ACTION). Which operation can violate referential integrity?

options.why: Reversed the direction; removing a referencing row never breaks a reference.

options.text: Inserting an Emp row whose did is NULL.
options.why: A NULL foreign key needs no match, so it is allowed unless did is declared NOT NULL.

options.text: Inserting a new row into Dept.
options.why: Reversed the direction; adding a referenced value cannot leave a dangling reference.

options.text: Deleting a Dept row whose did appears in Emp.
options.why: Emp rows would then point to a department that no longer exists.

questions.solution:
1. Violations come from the referencing side gaining an unmatched value or the referenced side losing a used value.
2. Deleting a referenced Dept row is the only such operation here.

questions.stem: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E, F) has exactly two candidate keys: {A, B} and {C}. How many superkeys does R have?

traps.why: Added 16 + 32 without subtracting the 8 supersets of {A, B, C}.
Counted only supersets of {C}.
Counted candidate keys instead of superkeys.

questions.solution:
1. Supersets of {A, B}: $2^4 = 16$.
2. Supersets of {C}: $2^5 = 32$.
3. Supersets of {A, B, C}: $2^3 = 8$.
4. 16 + 32 - 8 = 40.

questions.stem: Table R(A, B) is declared with `PRIMARY KEY (A, B)` and holds one row (1, 2). Each insertion below is tried separately on this table. Which succeed?

options.why: The pair (2, 2) is new; B may repeat when A differs.
Entity integrity forbids NULL in any primary key attribute.
Duplicates the existing key value (1, 2).
The pair (1, 3) differs from (1, 2); a composite key only needs the whole pair to be unique.

questions.solution:
1. A composite primary key requires the combination to be unique and every part NOT NULL.
2. (1, 3) and (2, 2) are new combinations; (NULL, 2) has a NULL; (1, 2) repeats.

questions.stem:
Consider R(A, B) and S(B, C).

**R**

| A | B |
|---|---|
| 1 | a |
| 2 | b |
| 3 | a |
| 4 | c |

**S**

| B | C |
|---|---|
| a | x |
| a | y |
| b | z |
| d | w |

How many tuples are in $R \bowtie S$ (natural join)?

traps.why: Counted the R tuples that find a match; B = a matches two S tuples, so each such R tuple appears twice.
Took the Cartesian product; the natural join keeps only pairs with equal B.
Counted R tuples with a match but dropped one of the a-rows.

questions.solution:
1. B = a: 2 R tuples × 2 S tuples = 4.
2. B = b: 1 × 1 = 1.
3. B = c and B = d: no partner.
4. Total 5.

traps.why: Counted the selected rows; π returns a set, so A = 1 and A = 2 appear once each.
Read $\lor$ as AND; only (1,4,1) and (4,3,1) satisfy both conditions.
Used B ≥ 2; the row (3, 2, 0) has B = 2, which fails B > 2.

questions.stem:
Using the same R(A, B) and S(B, C):

**R**

| A | B |
|---|---|
| 1 | a |
| 2 | b |
| 3 | a |
| 4 | c |

**S**

| B | C |
|---|---|
| a | x |
| a | y |
| b | z |
| d | w |

How many tuples are in the **full outer join** of R and S on B?

traps.why: Padded only the unmatched R tuple (4, c); a full outer join also keeps S's unmatched (d, w).
Computed the inner join only.
Added |R| + |S| as if every tuple were padded separately; matched tuples combine, and B = a produces 2 × 2 rows.

questions.solution:
1. Inner join: 5 tuples.
2. Unmatched R: (4, c) -> 1 tuple padded with NULL.
3. Unmatched S: (d, w) -> 1 tuple.
4. Total 7.

questions.stem: R(A, B) has 10 tuples and S(B, C) has 6 tuples. B is the primary key of S. What is the **maximum** possible number of tuples in $R \bowtie S$?

options.why: Bounded by the smaller relation; many R tuples may share the same B and join the same S tuple.
Ignored the key; 60 is possible only when B repeats in S.
Added the sizes as for a union; a join pairs tuples.
Each R tuple matches at most one S tuple because B is a key of S.

questions.solution:
1. Each R tuple has at most one partner in S (key).
2. So |R ⋈ S| ≤ |R| = 10, reached when every B value of R exists in S.

questions.stem:
R(A, B) and S(A, B) are union-compatible.

**R**

| A | B |
|---|---|
| 1 | x |
| 2 | y |
| 3 | x |

**S**

| A | B |
|---|---|
| 2 | y |
| 3 | y |
| 4 | x |

Which expressions return exactly 2 tuples?

options.why: Matched on A only (2 and 3); (3, x) ≠ (3, y), so only (2, y) is common.
(1, x) and (3, x) are in R but not in S.
Projection first collapses both to {x, y}, so the difference is empty.

questions.stem: R(A) = {1, 2, 3, 4} and S(C) = {2, 3, 5}. How many tuples are in the theta join $R \bowtie_{A < C} S$?

traps.why: Used A ≤ C; the pairs (2, 2) and (3, 3) fail the strict condition.
Took the full Cartesian product without applying the condition.
Reversed the comparison and counted A > C.

questions.stem:
**Enroll**

| sid | cid |
|---|---|
| s1 | c1 |
| s1 | c2 |
| s1 | c3 |
| s2 | c1 |
| s2 | c3 |
| s3 | c1 |
| s3 | c2 |
| s4 | c2 |

**Req**

| cid |
|---|
| c1 |
| c2 |

How many tuples are in $\text{Enroll} \div \text{Req}$?

traps.why: Kept students who took at least one required course (∃ instead of ∀).
Kept only students whose course set equals Req exactly (s3); division allows extra courses such as s1's c3.
Kept students who took c1 (s1, s2, s3) and ignored c2.

questions.solution:
1. s1: c1 ✓, c2 ✓.
2. s2: no c2.
3. s3: c1 ✓, c2 ✓.
4. s4: no c1.
5. Result {s1, s3}: 2 tuples.

questions.stem: Which expression equals $R(A, B) \div S(B)$?

options.why: Swapped the operands of the inner difference; that removes a values having a B outside S.
(π_A(R) × S) − R lists the missing (a, b) pairs; removing their a values leaves those with no missing pair.
Returns a values paired with at least one b in S, not with all of them.
This is the set of all candidate pairs, the first step of the formula, not the quotient.

questions.solution:
1. Build every candidate pair π_A(R) × S.
2. Subtract R to get the missing pairs.
3. Remove their A values from π_A(R).

questions.stem:
Enroll(sid, cid) is the table below and Req(cid) is **empty**.

**Enroll**

| sid | cid |
|---|---|
| s1 | c1 |
| s1 | c2 |
| s1 | c3 |
| s2 | c1 |
| s2 | c3 |
| s3 | c1 |
| s3 | c2 |
| s4 | c2 |

How many tuples are in $\text{Enroll} \div \text{Req}$, computed with $\pi_{sid}(\text{Enroll}) - \pi_{sid}\big((\pi_{sid}(\text{Enroll}) \times \text{Req}) - \text{Enroll}\big)$?

traps.why: Assumed an empty divisor gives an empty result; 'takes every course in an empty set' is vacuously true.
Counted the tuples of Enroll instead of distinct sid values.
Reused the answer for Req = {c1, c2}.

questions.solution:
1. π_sid(Enroll) × ∅ = ∅.
2. ∅ − Enroll = ∅, so nothing is subtracted.
3. Result = π_sid(Enroll) = {s1, s2, s3, s4}: 4 tuples.

questions.stem:
Supplies(sid, pid) records which supplier supplies which part; Parts(pid, color).

What does $\text{Supplies} \div \pi_{pid}\big(\sigma_{color = 'red'}(\text{Parts})\big)$ return?

options.text: sid of suppliers who supply every part
options.why: Dropped the σ; the divisor contains red parts only.

options.text: sid of suppliers who supply every red part
options.why: The divisor is the set of red parts; division keeps sid values paired with all of them.

options.text: sid of suppliers who supply only red parts
options.why: Reversed the inclusion; division allows a supplier to supply non-red parts too.

options.text: sid of suppliers who supply at least one red part
options.why: That is a join followed by projection (∃), not division (∀).

questions.solution:
1. Divisor = all red pids.
2. Division keeps sid with (sid, p) ∈ Supplies for every red p.
3. Extra non-red parts do not matter.

questions.stem: For relations R and S with suitable schemas and conditions p, q on R's attributes, which equivalence always holds?

options.why: Selections cascade: a row passes both filters exactly when it satisfies p ∧ q.
π does not distribute over −: a tuple of R − S can share its A value with a tuple of S.
After π_A the attribute B no longer exists, so the selection cannot be pushed above the projection.
Swapped ∪ and ∩; OR corresponds to union.

questions.solution:
1. Cascade of σ: σ_{p∧q} = σ_p ∘ σ_q.
2. σ_{p∨q} = σ_p ∪ σ_q.
3. π distributes over ∪ but not over − or ∩.

questions.stem: R and S are union-compatible. Which expressions are **always** equal to $R \cap S$?

options.why: Removing only R − S from the union leaves S, not R ∩ S.
S − R has no tuple of R, so this is just R.
Same identity with the roles swapped; ∩ is symmetric.
R − S removes the tuples not in S; taking those away from R leaves the common tuples.

questions.solution:
1. R − (R − S) = R ∩ S, and symmetrically S − (S − R).
2. (R ∪ S) − (R − S) = S.
3. R − (S − R) = R.

questions.stem:
Student(sid, name, dept), Enrolled(sid, cid, grade), Course(cid, title, credits).

What does $\pi_{name}\big(\sigma_{credits > 3 \,\land\, grade = 'A'}(\text{Student} \bowtie \text{Enrolled} \bowtie \text{Course})\big)$ return?

options.text: Names of students who got grade A in at least one course of at least 3 credits
options.why: Read > as ≥; a 3-credit course does not qualify.

options.text: Names of students who got grade A in at least one course of more than 3 credits
options.why: Each joined tuple is one enrolment; σ needs that same enrolment to have grade A and credits > 3.

options.text: Names of students who got grade A in every course of more than 3 credits
options.why: σ followed by π is existential; 'every' needs division.

options.text: Names of students who got an A in some course and took some (possibly other) course of more than 3 credits
options.why: Both conditions are tested on the same joined tuple, so they refer to the same course.

questions.solution:
1. The join pairs each enrolment with its student and course.

questions.stem: An analyst views sales by city and then switches to sales by country. Which OLAP operation is this?

options.why: Moving up the location hierarchy (city -> country) aggregates the data.
Reversed: drill-down goes from coarse to fine (country -> city).
Pivot only rotates the axes of the view.
Slice fixes one dimension to a single value; the level of detail does not change.

questions.solution:
1. Roll-up: climb a concept hierarchy (or drop a dimension).
2. Drill-down: the reverse.

questions.stem: On a cube with dimensions time, location and item, an analyst selects time = Q1, location ∈ {Delhi, Mumbai} and item ∈ {TV, phone}. Which operation is this?

options.why: No aggregation to a coarser level happens.
Restricting several dimensions to value sets gives a sub-cube.
Slice fixes a single dimension to one value; here three dimensions are restricted.
No move to a finer level happens.

questions.solution:
1. Slice: one dimension = one value -> (n − 1)-D view.
2. Dice: conditions on two or more dimensions -> sub-cube.

questions.stem: Which ordering is a valid concept hierarchy for location, from the most detailed to the most general level?

options.why: This lists the levels from general to detailed.
Reversed street and city: a city contains streets.
Skipped the containment order: a city lies inside a state.
Each street lies in one city, each city in one state, each state in one country.

questions.solution:
1. A concept hierarchy maps low-level values to higher-level concepts.
2. Location: street -> city -> state -> country.

questions.stem: A star schema has one fact table and four dimension tables: Time, Location, Product, Customer. It is snowflaked: Location is split into Location, City and State tables, and Product into Product and Category tables. How many tables does the snowflake schema have?

traps.why: Counted the original star schema only.
Counted the new tables but dropped the fact table or one original dimension.
Kept the original Location and Product tables and also added all their snowflaked tables; Location and Product are each one of the split tables.

questions.solution:
1. Fact: 1.
2. Time 1, Customer 1.
3. Location 3, Product 2.
4. Total 8.

questions.stem:
Sales(region, product, year, amount) has 4 regions, 3 products and 2 years, and every (region, product, year) combination occurs in the table. How many rows does this query return?

```sql
SELECT region, product, year, SUM(amount)
FROM Sales
GROUP BY CUBE (region, product, year);
```

options.why: Counted grouping sets ($2^3$), not rows.
Each dimension contributes its values plus the 'all' (NULL) value: (4+1)(3+1)(2+1).
Counted only the base grouping (region, product, year).
Left out the grand-total row (all three columns NULL).

questions.solution:
1. CUBE = all $2^3$ grouping sets.
2. Rows = Σ over sets of Π(values) = Π(nᵢ + 1).
3. 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

questions.stem:
**Sales**

| city | item | qty |
|---|---|---|
| Delhi | TV | 5 |
| Delhi | Phone | 3 |
| Pune | TV | 2 |
| Pune | TV | 4 |
| Agra | Laptop | 1 |

How many rows does this query return?

```sql
SELECT city, item, SUM(qty)
FROM Sales
GROUP BY CUBE (city, item);
```

traps.why: Used (3+1)(3+1); that holds only when every (city, item) pair occurs, but only 4 of the 9 pairs do.
Forgot the grand-total row.
Counted table rows; (Pune, TV) appears twice but forms one group.

questions.solution:
1. (city, item): 4 distinct pairs.
2. (city): 3. (item): 3. (): 1.
3. Total 4 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 11.

questions.stem: A data cube has 4 dimensions and no concept hierarchies. How many cuboids (group-by combinations), including the apex and base cuboids, does it have?

traps.why: Left out the apex cuboid (the grand total, grouping by nothing).
Counted dimensions instead of subsets of dimensions.
Counted orderings (4!) instead of subsets; a group-by does not depend on column order.

questions.solution:
1. Each cuboid = a subset of the 4 dimensions.
2. $2^4 = 16$.

questions.stem: A cube has three dimensions with concept hierarchies: time (day < month < year), item (item < type) and location (city < country). Counting the 'all' level for each dimension, how many cuboids does the cube have?

traps.why: Used $2^3$, ignoring the hierarchy levels.
Multiplied the level counts 3 × 2 × 2 and forgot the 'all' level of each dimension.
Added the per-dimension choices 4 + 3 + 3 instead of multiplying them.

questions.stem:
Sales(year, quarter, amount) contains data for 2 years and all 4 quarters of each. How many rows does this query return?

```sql
SELECT year, quarter, SUM(amount)
FROM Sales
GROUP BY ROLLUP (year, quarter);
```

traps.why: Used the CUBE formula (2+1)(4+1); ROLLUP has no (quarter) grouping set.
Forgot the grand-total row.
Counted only the base grouping (year, quarter).

questions.solution:
1. ROLLUP(year, quarter) = {(year, quarter), (year), ()}.
2. Rows: 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.

questions.stem: Income ranges from ₹12,000 to ₹98,000. Using min-max normalization to [0, 1], what is the normalized value of ₹73,600? (Give 3 decimals.)

traps.why: Divided by the maximum only (73600 / 98000).
Subtracted the minimum but divided by the maximum instead of the range.
Measured from the maximum: (98000 − 73600) / 86000.

questions.stem: Income has mean ₹54,000 and standard deviation ₹16,000. What is the z-score of ₹73,600?

traps.why: Subtracted in the wrong order (μ − v).
Divided the value by σ without subtracting the mean.
Divided the deviation 19,600 by the mean instead of σ.

questions.stem: The attribute values are 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9. Using the **population** standard deviation (divide by n), what is the z-score of 9?

options.why: Mean 5, variance 32/8 = 4, σ = 2, so z = (9 − 5)/2 = 2.
Stopped at the deviation 9 − 5 without dividing by σ.
Divided by the variance 4 instead of σ = 2.
Used the sample standard deviation (divide by n − 1 = 7), against the stated convention.

questions.stem: An attribute ranges from −986 to 917. Normalization by decimal scaling divides every value by $10^j$. What is the smallest valid j?

options.why: Scaled to 9.86, which is not below 1.
Leaves values near 98.6.
Valid but not the smallest; 0.0986 over-shrinks the data.

questions.stem: Sorted values: 4, 8, 15, 21, 21, 24, 25, 28, 30, 34. They are split into 3 **equal-width** bins over [4, 34], each bin closed on the left and open on the right (the last bin includes 34). How many values fall in the last bin?

traps.why: Put 24 in the middle bin; the middle bin is [14, 24), so 24 starts the last bin.
Made bins of roughly equal counts (equal-frequency) instead of equal width.
Used width (34 − 4)/3 = 10 but started the last bin at 30.

questions.stem: Sorted prices: 4, 8, 9, 15, 21, 21, 24, 25, 26 are put into equal-frequency bins of 3 values each. After **smoothing by bin means**, what does the first bin become?

options.why: Bin 1 = {4, 8, 9}; its mean (4 + 8 + 9)/3 = 7 replaces each value.
Smoothed by the bin median.
Left the bin unchanged.
Smoothed by bin boundaries (each value to the nearer of 4 and 9).

questions.solution:
1. Equal-frequency bins: {4, 8, 9}, {15, 21, 21}, {24, 25, 26}.
2. Mean of bin 1 = 21/3 = 7.
3. Every value becomes 7.

questions.stem: How many different simple random samples **without replacement** (SRSWOR) of size 3 can be drawn from a table of 10 tuples (order does not matter)?

traps.why: Counted ordered draws with replacement ($10^3$).
Counted ordered draws (10 × 9 × 8); a sample is a set.
Multiplied 10 × 3.

questions.solution:
1. SRSWOR sample = subset of size 3.
2. $\binom{10}{3} = 120$.

questions.stem: A customer table has 1000 tuples: 600 in segment A, 300 in B and 100 in C. A **proportional stratified** sample of 50 tuples is drawn. How many come from segment C?

options.why: C is 10% of the data, so it gets 10% of 50.
Split the sample equally across the 3 strata (≈ 50/3).
Took 10% of 100 (C's size) instead of 10% of the sample.
Assumed a small stratum may be left out; stratified sampling draws from every stratum.

questions.stem: Which statements about sampling for data reduction are correct?

options.text: SRSWR can include the same tuple more than once.
options.why: Each drawn tuple is put back before the next draw.

options.text: Stratified sampling draws from every stratum, so rare groups are represented.
options.why: Each stratum gets its own sample.

options.text: A simple random sample always keeps the proportion of a rare class exactly.
options.why: Over-claim; SRS proportions vary by chance, which is why stratification is used.

options.text: Cluster sampling selects whole groups, such as entire disk pages.
options.why: Groups are sampled, and every tuple in a chosen group is kept.

questions.solution:
1. SRSWR: repeats possible.
2. Cluster: pick groups.
3. Stratified: sample within each stratum.
4. SRS only matches proportions on average.

questions.stem: A sample of 50 tuples is drawn **with replacement** (SRSWR) from a table of 1000 tuples. What is the probability that a particular tuple appears in the sample at least once? (Give 4 decimals.)

traps.why: Used the without-replacement value s/N = 50/1000.
Used the probability of being picked in a single draw.
Gave the probability of never being picked, $(0.999)^{50}$.

questions.solution:
1. P(not picked in one draw) = 1 − 1/1000.
2. P(never) = $0.999^{50} = 0.9512$.
3. P(at least once) = 0.0488.

questions.stem: Which data-reduction technique is **lossless** (the original data can be rebuilt exactly)?

options.text: A wavelet transform with small coefficients set to zero
options.why: Zeroed coefficients cannot be recovered; this is lossy.

options.text: Run-length encoding of a sorted column
options.why: Each (value, count) pair expands back to the exact original run.

options.text: PCA keeping only the top k principal components
options.why: Dropped components lose variance, so reconstruction is approximate.
The other 90% of tuples are gone.

questions.solution:
1. Lossless: encoding that is exactly invertible (run-length, dictionary coding).
2. PCA truncation, wavelet thresholding and sampling are lossy.
